name: The Humane League: grants to Open Wing Alliance groups, THL UK and US policy groups (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: by share of the result (chicken pain days) at the defaults: the grant to THL UK (UK commitments, switches, the cage ban and the breed case, 86%), the US policy grants (1%), and the Open Wing Alliance grants abroad (12%) split by Schedule F's grant regions (Sub-Saharan Africa 30%, South America 26%, Europe outside the UK 25%, East Asia 9%, Middle East and North Africa 6%, South Asia 4%), each region at a stand-in country (Ghana, Brazil, Poland, Indonesia, Egypt, India; the review names wins in Ghana and Indonesia, the 990 in Poland).
summary: The Humane League's grants of 2025 ($4.26 million), each counted as what the recipients did with the money: $1.76 million to Open Wing Alliance groups abroad for corporate cage-free and broiler campaigns (credited with the grants' share of the alliance's 2025 wins outside the US: 216 new cage-free policies, restored pledges such as REWE's, 18 broiler policies implemented), $2.15 million to The Humane League UK (Tesco's and Aldi's space commitments for 240 million broilers a year, won in its year and delivered since, UK hens moved out of cages, and its part in a UK cage ban and in the legal case against fast-growing breeds, both counted at their chance), and $0.35 million to US policy groups (defending state cage-free sales laws against federal preemption, and local food-policy wins). Each grant buys a small share of wins that many groups share, and every branch rests on counts or chances we judged, so all are discounted for missing data. The US sales laws and the UK cage ban count their compliance costs from the regulators' own analyses, which outweigh the hens' and sows' gain in those two branches. The biggest uncertainties are those costs, how much more space does for a broiler of a fast-growing breed (the UK space commitments are the largest branch), THL UK's share of the supermarket campaigns, the long shot of the breed case, and the hens behind an average new pledge abroad.

sections.title: In chicken pain days
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for every animal model. The shared SAD figures are Ambitious Impact's, which count each species' pain as a share of a person's with its own species weights. Here those weights come out and Rethink Priorities' go in, so every species is counted in days of a chicken's disabling pain. How a chicken compares with a person is the one animal slider.

rows.label: New cage-free policies won by Open Wing Alliance members, 2025

source.title: Open Wing Alliance, 2025 end-of-year review (The Humane League, 18 February 2026)
source.quote: 216 new cage-free policies are now secured, helping egg-laying hens out of cages

rows.explainer: The alliance's count for 2025 (with 18 broiler policies implemented, the 990's '234 new corporate commitments for chickens', more than 60 in Africa).

rows.label: Share of the alliance's wins outside the US
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The alliance's 82 members work in 72 countries; THL's own new commitments (1.6 million hens, annual report p. 3) belong to its own campaigns, and the review's named wins are in Ghana, Indonesia, Latvia and Europe. US wins belong to THL's own campaigns (another line), so they are taken out here and from the staff count below alike.

rows.label: Hens a year covered by an average new policy
rows.explainer: Our judgment: no tracker gives hens for the 216 policies. Anchors: the largest named, Agro Innova in Ghana, distributes about 15 million eggs a month (about 600,000 hens at some 300 eggs a hen-year); THL's four new commitments covered 1.6 million hens (large US and European firms); most of the alliance's policies are hotels, bakeries, restaurants and regional producers with a few thousand hens each. A skewed mix averages about 10,000.

rows.label: Share of those hens not yet cage-free when the policy was won
rows.explainer: Our judgment: outside the EU, UK and US nearly all hens are caged (Welfare Footprint's country compilation in Our World in Data's cage-free series), but some companies pledge when they already buy some cage-free eggs.

rows.label: Hens a year under the new pledges abroad, not yet cage-free
Share of the hens abroad in enriched rather than battery cages
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on Schedule F: Europe outside the UK took $426,310 of the $1.69 million of listed grants abroad (25%), and the EU has used enriched cages since 2012; Africa, Latin America and Asia use battery cages. Policies in Europe are fewer per dollar than in the Global South, hence 20%.

rows.explainer: Our judgment: each child who switches to soy milk on a parent's note is about 180 servings a school year, so dairy servings may be a large part of the count; the rest are mixed meals (plant-based event catering, bean patties). A dairy serving counts at the site's dairy figure, far below a mixed meal's.

rows.label: UK breed case: years until the change takes effect
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The Court of Appeal dismissed THL UK's appeal on 13 December 2024 ([2024] EWCA Civ 1560), so a breed change needs prosecutions or a new code under its reading; Defra's animal welfare strategy (December 2025) encourages slower-growing breeds with no deadline and aims to finish its reforms by 2030. The cage ban's own path (consultation 2026, phase-out to 2032) shows the pace: a breed change across the industry takes most of a decade, 8 years, from 5 to 15.

rows.label: Chance a cage ban becomes law (England, then the devolved nations)

source.title: The Humane League UK, An historic moment for farmed animals (22 December 2025)
source.quote: A consultation is not a ban, but it is a critical step forward.

rows.explainer: Our judgment. The government's Animal Welfare Strategy (22 December 2025) committed to consult on ending cages, and the consultation opened in January 2026 with a six-year phase-out; consultations usually lead to rules, but the egg industry opposes the timeline and parliamentary time is short. One event, drawn as happening or not.

rows.label: Chance the legal route ends fast-growing breeds in the UK

source.title: The Humane League UK, annual report and accounts, year to 31 March 2025
source.quote: they ruled in favour of our main argument - that the law says that animals should not be kept in the UK if it means they will suffer because of how they have been bred

rows.explainer: Our judgment. The Court of Appeal rejected THL UK's appeal but agreed that the law forbids keeping animals that suffer because of how they were bred; THL UK plans private prosecutions on that reading. Such cases rarely change a whole industry: about 1 in 30 within the years counted. One event, drawn as happening or not.

rows.label: Chance federal preemption of the state sales laws passes, without the year's opposition
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/farm_animal_laws.json): the EATS Act's language and the 'Save Our Bacon' Act were in the House Farm Bill drafts of 2024-25; without the coalition's opposition (letters from more than 200 members of Congress) passage in the next Farm Bill is put at 30%, from 10% to 50%. One event, drawn as happens or doesn't; the opposition removes a share of it (next row).

rows.label: Share of the preemption risk the year's opposition removed
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts/farm_animal_laws.json), one number in every model of the same fight: the year's opposition takes about 5 points off a 30% risk, a sixth of it; a share of the risk, so it never raises it.

rows.label: THL UK's share of the campaigners' resources behind the space commitments
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Five groups press UK supermarkets on broiler standards: THL UK (Co-op's AGM, Lidl's 'Shop of Horrors', Tesco), Open Cages, Animal Equality UK, the RSPCA and Compassion in World Farming (whose ChickenTrack tracks them). Only Waitrose and M&S have signed the full Better Chicken Commitment; most others have taken only its 30 kg/m² space rule (The Grocer, March 2026), the commitments counted here, which followed THL UK's supermarket campaigns. An equal split would be 20%; THL UK led these two, so 35%, from 15% to 60%.

rows.explainer: Our judgment: three groups follow UK cage-free pledges (THL UK's corporate relations team, Compassion in World Farming's EggTrack, the RSPCA); an equal split would be a third, and THL UK's direct pressure on slipping companies a little less than that: 30%, from 15% to 50%.

THL UK's public affairs is one post and its supporters' emails: 3%, from 1% to 8%.

rows.explainer: Our judgment: THL UK brought the case (with Advocates for Animals) and the appeal fell in its year, so its share is above its share of the cage ban (0.03 among about ten groups over five years); but a later win would need further cases and other groups' work over most of a decade, so a year's share is small. 0.05, range 0.01-0.2.

Side effect: stronger groups win more later
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as a share of the modelled result: the grants build groups (first-time grantees in Australia, Chile, Colombia, Hungary, Indonesia and Italy) and defend activists in court (the Animal Activist Legal Defense Project gift), whose later wins aren't in this year's count. No study measures how much new groups win later, so there is no reference class; 10%, from 0 to 40%, wide for that reason.

rows.label: Side effect: pledges and wins spill over to laws and suppliers
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as a share of the modelled result: won pledges make cage-free laws easier to pass (Massachusetts' Question 3 in 2016 and California's Proposition 12 in 2018 followed the 2015-16 wave of corporate pledges and wrote the same standard into law; in the EU, End the Cage Age has not yet led to a law) and push suppliers to convert barns that also serve buyers without a pledge. 10%, from 0 to 30%.

rows.label: Side effect: cage eggs sold elsewhere, and dearer eggs
rows.explainer: Our judgment, as a share of the modelled result, anchored on the shared figure for eggs (@sad_factors.cage_crate_market_leakage_share: −10%, from Norwood and Lusk's 0.91 eggs per egg not bought): cage eggs a pledged buyer stops taking can be sold to others, and dearer cage-free eggs move a few buyers to chicken meat, more animals per calorie. For the broilers given more space (the largest branch), dearer chicken moves some buyers to other chicken or to pork, and fewer birds are raised for the same meat; the two roughly offset, so the range is widened both ways: −10%, from −30% to +5%.

rows.label: Side effects, as a share of the modelled result
rows.explainer: The sum of the three side-effect rows above, each weighted by the shared side-effect slider.
